## The finish line

By the end of this course you can walk a single unit of blood from the moment a donor is
recruited to the moment it is transfused into a patient, name the regulated step at every
stage, and say which system — BECS, LIS, or HIS — touches it and why.

That's the whole point of putting this course first. You can't govern a system you can't
place in the workflow, and you can't push back on a vendor, a Quality Analyst, or an
inspector about a step you can't describe.

## Before you start

This course assumes the three foundations, which are short and already built:

- [Reading a CFR citation](../../foundations/reading-a-cfr-citation/index.qmd) — so a
  citation in a lesson is something you can read aloud and act on, not a string of numbers.
- [Regulatory landscape orientation](../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd)
  — so you can tell an FDA regulation from FDA guidance from an AABB standard, and say
  which one binds.
- [Risk and controls vocabulary](../../foundations/risk-and-controls-vocabulary/index.qmd)
  — so likelihood, severity, detectability, and preventive/detective/corrective mean one
  thing here and everywhere later.

If you skipped them, start there. Every module below leans on all three.

## The five modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **Donor recruitment and screening** — walk a donor from recruitment through registration,
   health history, and the eligibility decision, and name the record that proves the decision
   was made correctly.
2. **Collection and testing** — follow a donation from the needle through the required
   infectious-disease and blood-typing panel, and explain why nothing leaves quarantine until
   every result is in.
3. **Component processing and labeling** — explain how one donation becomes several products
   with different shelf lives, and read an ISBT 128 label well enough to say what each part of
   it guarantees.
4. **Storage, distribution, and hemovigilance** — track a released unit through storage,
   shipping, and the hospital transfusion service to the patient, and say what has to happen,
   and be reported, when something goes wrong.
5. **BECS in the pipeline** — point at every place Blood Establishment Computer Software
   touches the pipeline, and say in two sentences to your CIO why it isn't governed like a
   normal enterprise application.

Modules one through four build the pipeline in order. Module five goes back over the same
pipeline with the systems map laid on top, which is where this course hands off to the
validation and BECS track later.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
